resources.string: Welcome to Rún

Messaging with nothing to seize, trace, or subpoena — no accounts, no numbers, no trail. The name is Old Norse: \"rún\" — secret, hidden knowledge, the root of \"rune\", and in Irish and Scottish Gaelic the beloved trusted to keep it.
Routed through Tor

Everything Rún sends rides Tor — a global network that relays your traffic through several hops, hiding your IP and location. Not even Rún\'s own relay learns who or where you are, and Rún connects no other way.
Red means Tor
Watch the runestone — red means you\'re on Tor. Its ring pulses harder the closer you get, holds solid red the moment the relay answers, and then the R lights.
End-to-end encrypted
Every message is sealed with a key only you and your contact hold, and as you keep chatting that key ratchets forward — so exposing a single key still leaves the rest sealed.
A relay that can\'t read

Rún\'s relay is deliberately dumb — no accounts, nothing to read, just padded blobs in numbered inboxes it passes along, their padded size revealing nothing about the contents. Nothing lingers once it\'s delivered — messages clear from the inbox as you read them, and the inbox itself is reclaimed after a long stretch of silence.
White ᚱ means Relay
When the ᚱ at its centre burns white, Rún has reached the relay — messages can send and arrive. Red without the white ᚱ means Tor is up but the relay isn\'t reachable yet.
Contacts you choose

No emails, no sign-ups — and no stranger can add you. You meet in person and scan each other\'s QR. Each contact gets a random codename; add a private note only you can see, so only you know who they really are.
Vouched introductions

There\'s no directory of who\'s on Rún. Instead, someone you already trust can introduce you to someone they trust — and you choose whether to accept. Trust travels person to person, never through a server.
Group chats

A group lives only on its members\' phones — no group account, no member list, nothing on the relay to seize. Each message is sent privately to every member, so the relay never learns the group\'s name, who\'s in it, or a word of what\'s said. It does see one message go to several inboxes at once — enough to tell a group exists and how many it reached, never whose.
Messages vanish
This is \"burn on read\": messages live in memory alone, never on disk. Close the app or leave a chat, and they\'re gone for good.
Quiet by default

No ads, analytics, or profiles — ever, and out of the box no notifications: Rún reaches its relay, over Tor, only when you open it. You can opt into instant alerts — a contentless wake carried by Apple\'s or Google\'s push service, or by one you install yourself, revealing only rough timing, never the message or who sent it — off unless you turn it on.
Locks and wipes itself

Left idle or sent to the background, Rún locks — you unlock again with your PIN or passphrase. Too many wrong tries, or a long stretch untouched, goes further: it erases the keys and all data, beyond recovery. How soon each happens is set by the protection level you choose.
Screen privacy
Screenshots, screen recording, and the recent-apps preview are all blocked, so nothing leaks to your gallery or the app switcher.
The app-switcher preview and screen recording are covered. iOS can\'t block a manual screenshot, so take care with sensitive chats — Rún warns you if one is taken.
Forensic-safe

A seized phone gives up nothing useful. Everything at rest is sealed with SQLCipher, and a wipe erases the keys themselves — leaving only noise, no caches or fragments. How hard it is to open is your choice: Decent leans on your PIN; Secure binds the key to this phone\'s security chip, behind your fingerprint or face; Maximum swaps the PIN for a passphrase only you know — so even a fully imaged phone stays shut.
Ready when you are
That\'s Rún — quiet, private, and yours to keep secret. Add someone in person, and start a conversation no one else can see.
Rún has no ads, no investors, and never sells your data. Every donation — large or small — helps keep it free for everyone, forever.
Notifications travel through %1$s’s servers. They never contain your messages — only that a new one is waiting for you.

The relay sends a contentless wake through %1$s — no sender, no text, no count — and Rún shows a generic “Notification”. Nothing is fetched or decrypted until you open Rún and unlock. %3$s works the same way; neither vendor is more private.\n\nThe relay learns something too: all your inboxes register under the one push address %2$s issued to this phone, so the relay can tell which conversations share a device. Someone able to compel both %2$s and the relay could link you to your conversations. That is why this switch is off until you turn it on.
%1$s only learns when messages reach you — never who sent them or what they say. Over time, those timestamps alone can show when you communicate.

A wake fires each time a message reaches you, so %1$s sees a running pattern — how often, at what hours — tied to this phone’s Rún install. Tor normally hides that timing; turning notifications on trades some of it for instant delivery.
Your messages never reach %1$s. Rún fetches them over Tor and decrypts them on this phone only after you unlock.

The wake carries nothing and triggers no network activity by itself. Your messages wait encrypted on the relay until you open Rún, which fetches them over Tor and decrypts them locally with the key derived from your PIN or passphrase. %1$s never receives, stores or relays a single message byte.

This phone has no Google services, so a separate app you choose — a UnifiedPush distributor such as ntfy — delivers the wake signal.

The distributor app keeps one connection open to a push server and hands each wake to Rún. Nothing about your messages changes: the wake carries no message, and Rún still fetches and decrypts everything over Tor after you unlock.
Two parties learn when you are contacted — the distributor app and its push server — never who wrote or what. Those timestamps alone can show when you communicate.

That is one party more than the Google build has. The distributor sees every wake because it delivers them; its push server sees them because it forwards them and, on a public server, also sees this phone’s IP address. Neither sees a sender, a message or a count. Tor normally hides that timing; notifications trade some of it for instant delivery. Run your own push server and the second party is you.
Your messages never reach the distributor or its server. Each wake is encrypted to this phone and carries nothing; Rún fetches your messages over Tor and decrypts them after you unlock.

Every wake is encrypted to a key pair that never leaves this phone (Web Push, RFC 8291), so nobody who learns your endpoint can forge a new alert — though your push server could replay one you already received, Rún limits how often a repeat can trigger the banner — and every wake is the same fixed size. Your messages wait encrypted on the relay until you open Rún, which fetches them over Tor and decrypts them locally with the key derived from your PIN or passphrase.

Six digit pin code for opening Rún. Can be brute forced by forensic tools in hours, so Rún relies fully on the phone protection. On Android, keyboard suggestions and emoji stay on, so the keyboard may learn words you type.

Six digit pin code, but the vault key is sealed in the phone\'s security chip and released only by your fingerprint or face. A seized phone resists forensic brute-forcing even if its passcode is cracked. On Android, keyboard suggestions and emoji stay on, so the keyboard may learn words you type.

A long passphrase instead of a pin code — strong enough that no forensic tool can brute force it, even from an unlocked phone. The keyboard runs in password mode: nothing you type is learned or suggested, and on Android the emoji key is unavailable.
Your phone has no %1$s

Without one, your passphrase is the only thing between your messages and anyone holding this phone. So Rún runs at Maximum here.

It asks for that passphrase every time, locks after 60 seconds idle, and the next time Rún is opened after 7 days without use, it erases everything — permanently.

Set a passcode on your phone to choose a gentler level.
